stories.headline: In Mauricio Pochettino, Manchester United have finally hired a proper manager
stories.summary: After years of near-misses, Man United have finally landed Mauricio Pochettino, a manager with the kind of pedigree, class and credibility the club have been looking for.
stories.body:
Mauricio Pochettino is the coach that Manchester United have needed for a decade, but it sums up the dysfunctional nature of the Premier League's biggest club that they have only now hired a guy they rejected three times before.

Will it be better late than never? That's what United will be desperately hoping after persuading Pochettino to turn his back on the United States job to replace Michael Carrick as manager at Old Trafford.

Taking charge at United comes with plenty of problems on and off the pitch for Pochettino. But, after so many near misses -- he was on the verge of taking the top job three times since 2019 -- maybe he really is the right man at the right time for a club that has been locked in a downward spiral for longer than any of their supporters cares to remember.

What made Pochettino the right man for Man United

The 54-year-old, who built an exciting young team at Tottenham Hotspur before stints at Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and the USMNT, was the "next big thing" the first time he was overlooked by United in favor of José Mourinho in 2016. And while the stars have now finally aligned for United and Pochettino, there is still an element of farce about the appointment.

Had United resisted the temptation to hand Carrick a two-year deal at the end of last season and move for Pochettino, they could have landed him for nothing at the end of the World Cup. But they have instead had to make a $10 million compensation payment to the U.S. Soccer Federation following his decision to sign a four-year contract extension in August.

Pochettino's release fee will be a timely reminder to United, however, that pedigree and experience are worth paying for. Not since they hired Mourinho in 2016 to go toe-to-toe with Pep Guardiola at Manchester City have United turned to a coach with a proven record in the Premier League and Champions League.

Since dismissing Mourinho in December 2018 following the souring of his relationship with the dressing room and boardroom, United have gambled on either former players with no managerial credentials -- Ole Gunnar Solskjær and Carrick -- or rising coaches with no body of work in a major European league, like Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim. But by appointing Pochettino, United have finally learned that inexpensive and inexperienced hires are quickly chewed up and spat out by the Old Trafford meat grinder.

It has never been a job for a novice, and Pochettino is United's first credible appointment since Mourinho. This matters at a club of United's magnitude.

The supporters need to be convinced by the manager's track record and so do the players. When each of Pochettino's recent predecessors have hit the turbulence of bad results, he has been unable to arrest the slump by motivating the players who have, almost like clockwork, lost faith and respect in the manager and taken advantage of his weakness.

In Pochettino, United's players will see on the sideline a coach who has worked at the biggest clubs and with the best players -- Harry Kane, Lionel Messi, Kylian Mbappé. The Argentine is also somebody who has built a team capable of challenging for the Premier League and Champions League at Spurs.

None of Solskjær, Ten Hag, Amorim or Carrick had the same status; they lacked the ability to unite a squad behind them. But Pochettino -- most notably with Spurs and the USMNT at this year's World Cup -- has shown he can forge a team spirit and togetherness that has been absent from Old Trafford arguably since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

But while Pochettino ends United's search for a convincing coach, he still has a huge task ahead of him to breathe new life into the club. There is ongoing hostility from the supporters toward both ownership groups, the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe's Ineos Group, and finances are so tight at United that money for new signings in January will be extremely limited.

Pochettino also inherits a squad built by six different managers -- Luke Shaw, who played for Pochettino at Southampton, was signed by Louis van Gaal in 2014 -- so it will take time and patience to mold such a disparate group of players into a functioning team. But United at least now have a coach in Pochettino who has walked the walk before, and that is crucial for a club in such dire need of assurance, leadership and clear direction.

stories.headline: Need fantasy football lineup or trade advice? Join our live Q&A with our expert, noon ET
stories.summary: ESPN fantasy football expert Eric Moody is here to answer your pressing questions live from noon to 1 p.m. ET.
stories.body:
Join the chat as ESPN fantasy football expert Eric Moody will be here to answer all of your start/sit questions and other fantasy-related queries, live from noon to 1 p.m. ET every Friday of the NFL's regular season.

What's the latest injury buzz as kickoff time approaches? Which player is the better bet for your flex spot? Should you be considering a trade to upgrade your roster? Ask away! Our expert will try to answer as many questions as he can to get you ready for this week's action.

Week 10 Rankings | Clay's Playbook | Cockcroft's matchup rankings

Why is my question not getting answered?

Once submitted, your question does not automatically get posted in the chat. Our moderators select which questions they wish to answer and are trying to avoid repeat questions or topics. Scroll back to see if perhaps your question (or one very similar) was answered earlier in the chat.
We are receiving thousands of questions during our hourlong Q&A session and try to get to as many as we can. However, while we appreciate every submission, there is no way we can get to every question that comes in.

stories.headline: What's new in free agency? Lessons from 2026 MLB GM meetings
stories.summary: With a wild winter ahead, here are the top offseason priorities straight from every front office.
stories.byline: Jorge Castillo and Alden Gonzalez and Jesse Rogers
stories.body:
With an MLB lockout looming, baseball's top executives gathered in Las Vegas this week for the annual general managers meetings. Amid the uncertainty of this hot stove season, it was the first opportunity to hear officials from all 30 front offices discuss their priorities for the unique offseason ahead.

From the pursuit of top free agent ace Tarik Skubal to the various logistics teams are facing this winter, ESPN MLB reporters Jorge Castillo, Alden Gonzalez and Jesse Rogers report on what each franchise will be focused on over the next few months.

Jump to a team:

AL East: BAL | BOS | NYY | TB | TOR

AL Central: CHW | CLE | DET | KC | MIN

AL West: ATH | HOU | LAA | SEA | TEX

NL East: ATL | MIA | NYM | PHI | WSH

NL Central: CHC | CIN | MIL | PIT | STL

NL West: ARI | COL | LAD | SD | SF

AL East

Baltimore Orioles
The Orioles have encountered an uncomfortable reality after failing to reach the postseason for the second straight year: Their hyped young core of position players is not good enough.

They could augment the group by signing another free agent after landing Pete Alonso (the team's best player in 2026 by a large margin) last offseason. They could move on from other players in that nucleus after dealing Adley Rutschman, a former No. 1 pick and two-time All-Star, to the Red Sox at the trade deadline. For now, they're exploring both avenues, knowing they also need some internal development to return to contention.

"There's a ton of talent on this roster, so we just need to make sure we're getting the most out of it." Orioles general manager Jared Banner said. "Turning that talent into wins. We want our young players turning from being young players into superstars, and that's what it takes to really get better quickly."

Baltimore is also looking to address the starting rotation, with Trevor Rogers hitting free agency. The Orioles won't be vying for Skubal's or the free agent pitchers in the tier below that, but they're poised to add a midrotation hurler. -- Castillo

Boston Red Sox
The task isn't complicated for Red Sox president of baseball operations Craig Breslow. With a standout pitching staff that should have Garrett Crochet back and healthy in 2027, improving his club's offense is his top priority.

First baseman Willson Contreras, acquired last offseason from the Cardinals, enjoyed a career season with a .901 OPS and a 151 wRC+ that ranked third in the majors. Wilyer Abreu (112 wRC+) and Ceddanne Rafaela (110 wRC+) were key contributors while supplying elite outfield defense. But the Red Sox ranked 23rd in runs scored and 26th in home runs in the majors in 2026.

They're hunting for power before the expected lockout.

"The offense was inconsistent, and we need to look to find ways to score more runs," Breslow said. "I think some of that probably comes from guys like Roman [Anthony] and Curtis Mead and Adley [Rutschman] being healthy with us for full seasons. And then we will explore opportunities to improve the team with guys who currently aren't on the roster." -- Castillo

New York Yankees
The Yankees first have to figure out their coaching staff after bench coach Brad Ausmus left to become the Astros' manager, hitting coach James Rowson was let go and catching coach Tanner Swanson took the Mariners' bench coach job. Former Astros manager Joe Espada is among the candidates for bench coach, and former Dodgers co-hitting coach Aaron Bates is among the candidates for hitting coach, sources told ESPN.

After that, it's waiting to see whether closer David Bednar accepts the one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer by the Nov. 17 deadline. Bednar, 32, would undoubtedly garner a multiyear deal -- with the Yankees or another club -- if he declines the contract. But he could take it and hit free agency next winter without the weight of draft compensation hindering his market.

The Yankees are interested in signing left-hander Adrian Morejon -- the best free agent reliever -- if Bednar ends up elsewhere. Waiting for Bednar's decision, however, could hamper that pursuit. General manager Brian Cashman has avoided giving relievers big contracts in recent years, but he said this week that he's "not afraid to do it" should the opportunity surface.

Elsewhere, Cashman said he'd like a better right-handed-hitting catcher to partner with Austin Wells and "without a doubt" is looking to upgrade third base after Ryan McMahon's struggles in 2026. As it stands, Spencer Jones projects as the team's starting center fielder, but Cashman acknowledged Jones "probably profiles better on the corner." A right-handed-hitting center fielder to platoon with the left-handed-hitting Jones is another possibility. -- Castillo

Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays began their offseason after losing the World Series in five games by exercising Drew Rasmussen's $20 million club option for next season. It's ultimately a bargain for a pitcher in his prime who finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting and starred in the postseason, but history suggests the low-budget Rays would at least explore trading him to maximize value.

That, however, doesn't appear to be the case here, even though Rasmussen's $20 million salary would be the largest in franchise history. President of baseball operations Erik Neander said he does not plan on trading Rasmussen. Perhaps new ownership and an impending move to Tampa in 2029 could even prompt the Rays to extend their ace.

Rasmussen would anchor a rotation that could look very different next season. Nick Martinez, the Rays' other All-Star starter, and Freddy Peralta, who excelled after he was acquired at the trade deadline, are both free agents. Shane McClanahan, their former ace, is a trade candidate entering his final year of control after three injury-plagued years.

Peralta likely priced himself out of the Rays' comfort zone, but a reunion with Martinez, a clubhouse leader who shined in his first full season as a starter, is possible. They could also look to deepen their lineup, but the rotation is the priority. -- Castillo

Toronto Blue Jays
The Blue Jays have money and want to spend it.

A year after signing Dylan Cease to a seven-year, $210 million contract, Toronto is one of the few teams scheduled to meet with Tarik Skubal, who could sign for close to double Cease's deal. If Skubal isn't the answer, the Jays will look for starting pitching elsewhere.

Otherwise, the Blue Jays are looking to add a second baseman and a right-handed hitter. Outfielder Seiya Suzuki makes sense. They've expressed interest in second basemen Brandon Lowe and Jazz Chisholm Jr., two very different players coming off very different seasons.

Lowe had perhaps his best season with 35 home runs, an .824 OPS and a startling defensive improvement. Chisholm had a disappointing walk year for the Yankees and there are makeup concerns, but his talent is unquestionable two years removed from a 30-30 season. He's one of six players with at least 30 steals each of the past three seasons. Defensively, he grades out as elite at second base and above average at third base and center field -- all premium positions. -- Castillo

AL Central

Chicago White Sox
By the end of the year, White Sox reliever Grant Taylor was seemingly pitching multiple innings in every important game. He was more or less Chicago's version of Aaron Ashby, a valuable late-inning option.

Or at least he was.

"The plan is to put him in the rotation," GM Chris Getz said. "It's something that he's definitely wanted to do. We feel like it's the best time [to try it] for Grant and for us."

The White Sox have experience moving a star reliever to the rotation and getting the most out of him. Garrett Crochet used to be that guy. Now, it's Taylor's turn.

The team needs more in its rotation after running out of pitchers. Taylor and former first-round pick Noah Schultz will get an opportunity in 2027, along with whomever they acquire this offseason. -- Rogers

Cleveland Guardians
The end of the Guardians' 2026 season, which featured a strong final regular-season stretch and a playoff run that brought them two wins from the World Series, was informative. And because of it -- for once -- they're not as desperate to add hitting as they normally are.

"Overall, we didn't score enough runs, but we were much better after the trade deadline than we were before," president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti said. "Jo [Adell] and Nathaniel [Lowe] were responsible for that, but also the growth of our younger guys. That group is returning."

Antonetti is referring, of course, to outfielder Chase DeLauter, second baseman Travis Bazzana and surprisingly productive catcher Patrick Bailey.

The team will focus on deepening a pitching staff that nearly helped carry the club to the Fall Classic. The Guardians like their immediate future. -- Rogers

Detroit Tigers
The Tigers' president of baseball operations, Scott Harris, was barely done telling reporters about needing to fill some holes in the back end of his bullpen before signing righty reliever Emilio Pagan to a one-year deal.

Pagan can replace Kenley Jansen as that late-inning, veteran presence in Detroit.

After Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize moved on last summer, Harris admitted to having a lot of needs in the rotation as well. In a perfect world for Detroit, young starters such as Jackson Jobe, Troy Melton and newly acquired righty River Ryan aren't pushed past their limits in 2027.

"We think there is an opportunity to add more innings in some creative ways that help insulate these young starters from the demands of a full, major league season," Harris said. "We'll try to add pitching and be creative about it."

Harris checked off one box for the Tigers with Pagan's addition, but Detroit needs more in the cupboard. -- Rogers

Kansas City Royals
The Royals want to balance their lineup after finishing in the bottom third of the league against left-handed pitching last year. A right-handed-hitting outfielder would be a nice acquisition.

"Right-handed stands out," GM J.J. Picollo said. "We have a lot of left-handed hitters, particularly in the outfield, so a right-handed-hitting outfielder would be really helpful, especially if they can play center field a little bit."

Lane Thomas didn't finish the year for Kansas City, yet he led the Royals in home runs from right-handed-hitting outfielders. Pairing another dangerous hitter from the right side with Bobby Witt Jr. can only help balance things for the Royals.

Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena are the top hitters in free agency, but might price themselves out of Kansas City. -- Rogers

Minnesota Twins
Minnesota would like catcher Ryan Jeffers to return but is ready to pivot if it doesn't happen.

Jeffers was extended the qualifying offer and is exploring the market.

"We remain engaged with his group," GM Jeremy Zoll said. "We still have Victor Caratini, but he's not going to catch 162 games, so we'll have to find a complement for him and replace the loss of Jeffers' production."

Zoll said it has been "easy" to be candid with potential replacements at catcher, telling agents they're working through things with Jeffers.

If Jeffers and free agent Josh Bell move on, the Twins will look to augment an offense that produced during most of the summer -- with those two players helping lead the way. -- Rogers

AL West

Athletics
The 2026 A's ranked 29th in starters' ERA and last in bullpen ERA. Their pitching clearly still has not caught up to the promise of their position-player group, which could include top prospect Leo De Vries in 2027. But it doesn't seem as though this is an area the A's will attack aggressively in free agency this offseason.

New president of baseball operations Taylor Smith believes a lot of the pitchers' woes were a product of the hitter-friendly environment in Sacramento -- one the team will play in for only one more season -- and seems more focused on development at this point. The A's have an expensive veteran in Luis Severino, a controllable young starter in J.T. Ginn, two exciting prospects in Gage Jump and Jack Perkins, and a couple of more seasoned, out-of-options hurlers in Luis Medina and Jacob Lopez constituting their major league starting pitching depth at the moment.

That group probably won't change much. The difference between the A's expected ERA and actual ERA was a full run in 2026 -- 4.52 versus 5.53, respectively. -- Gonzalez

Houston Astros
One of Randy Flores' primary tasks as the Astros' new GM -- outside of addressing the team's starting-pitching depth -- will be unclogging the infield.

"The math is the math on that," Flores said, "and that's something that we really have to take a hard look at how we solve."

The Astros' current alignment would probably have Yordan Alvarez starting in left field to make all the pieces fit, a move that is certainly not ideal. Alvarez can go back to DH if the Astros simply trade one of Christian Walker, Isaac Paredes or Jeremy Pena because Carlos Correa and Jose Altuve are locked in at third and second base, respectively.

But Walker, Paredes and Pena are all under team control for only one more year. And the uncertainty of how many games -- if any -- will be played in 2027 makes it really difficult for teams to justify trading for players in that situation, industry sources said this week. Perhaps the Astros will swap one of those infielders for an outfielder or a starting pitcher who's also eligible for free agency after 2027, but in all likelihood, Houston probably won't find a match until after a new CBA is signed. -- Gonzalez

Los Angeles Angels
There might be no more awkward situation in baseball than that of the Angels. The new owners have yet to be approved, and the GM, John Mozeliak, is on a contract that expires at year's end, with full knowledge he won't be coming back. Mozeliak, the Cardinals' longtime head of baseball operations, likes to refer to himself as an "innkeeper" these days.

Barring some amazing, unforeseen opportunity they can't pass up, the Angels won't do anything substantive with their roster before the potential Dec. 1 lockout. Mozeliak's role at the GM meetings was basically to gather intel on the trade and free agent markets.

"And when new leadership gets in place," Mozeliak said, "share our notes and allow them to hit the ground running."

Whether that new leadership is in place before the end of the month remains to be seen. Prominent members of the new ownership group were in Las Vegas this week meeting with a broad range of candidates for their new head of baseball operations, working from a list Mozeliak said he did not fully put together.

Mozeliak expects to get involved once that list gets pared down. There is still no timetable for a vote on the transfer of the Angels from Arte Moreno to Stan Kroenke, but it is not expected to take place at next week's owners meetings. For now, the Angels are basically on pause.

"My role right now is to keep the lights on, keep the trains running on time, and that's what I'll do," Mozeliak said. -- Gonzalez

Seattle Mariners
The Mariners were arguably the most disappointing team in baseball this year, finishing 10 games below .500 in a season that began with World Series expectations. But their focus is not on blowing up the roster; it's on plugging specific holes and emphasizing development at the major league level for a lineup that doesn't possess any regulars older than 30.

It's what pushed them to hire the relatively unknown Jason Kanzler as their manager and pair him with former field coordinator Tyler Swanson as his bench coach.

The Mariners want to add another hitter or two, preferably right-handed, and are open to doing so for the left side of their infield or the outfield corners, with Brendan Donovan and Colt Emerson able to move around, according to a source.

The Mariners will also look for late-game bullpen help to form the bridge to closer Andres Munoz. The expectation is that they will plug some of those holes by moving at least one of their starting pitchers, with Bryce Miller, Emerson Hancock and George Kirby the more attainable ones, industry sources said. -- Gonzalez

Texas Rangers
There is no bigger question surrounding the Rangers this offseason than Corey Seager's future. The Rangers are open to trading him, according to industry sources. Finding a match is the tricky part. Seager is owed $155 million over the next five years and will play next season at 33 years old.

He remains an elite hitter, but his injury history -- he has averaged barely more than 110 games over the past four seasons, with ailments to his hip and back along the way -- has rival executives thinking that the Rangers would have a really hard time finding a team willing to take on the money and give up anything of substance.

Then there's the threat of a salary cap, which would make it difficult for high-payroll teams to justify absorbing that type of contract. And then there's the fact that Seager has now qualified for 10-and-5 rights, allowing him to block any trade. At this point, Seager would be open to approving one, a source with knowledge of his thinking said, but it would have to be the right fit. Whether that fit materializes before the lockout remains to be seen. -- Gonzalez

NL East

Atlanta Braves
Braves president of baseball operations Alex Anthopoulos plays things close to the vest, but starting pitching, shortstop and bullpen were Atlanta's clear areas of need entering the offseason. Atlanta gave the first multiyear free agent contract of the offseason to reliever Evan Phillips, who effectively replaces fellow free agent Raisel Iglesias.

Even with Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Bryce Elder, Reynaldo Lopez, Didier Fuentes, and Grant Holmes seemingly in the equation for next year, the Braves could use at least another viable starter behind ace Chris Sale. A reunion with Tyler Mahle, who was a revelation upon joining the Braves at the trade deadline, is possible. So is one with utilityman Mauricio Dubon.

"I don't look at timing," Anthopoulos said. "I don't get to pick. If someone's ready to make a trade today, we'll do it. If a free agent's ready to sign today, we'll certainly be engaged. You don't get to pick the timing of things. You'd love to go through stuff, but we'll just react as things come up." -- Castillo

Miami Marlins
The Marlins took another step forward in 2026, finishing in third place in the NL East with 80 wins despite carrying the second-smallest payroll in the majors.

The club picked up Sandy Alcántara's $21 million club option for 2027, his final year before reaching free agency, after the season. Miami won't be in the market to invest huge money in free agents, but the team has some flexibility, considering Alcántara is the only guaranteed salary on the Marlins' payroll for next season; everyone else under team control is either pre-arbitration or eligible for arbitration.

One clear area of need is the bullpen. This week, president of baseball operations Peter Bendix said he is looking to add a left-handed reliever. A year ago, he gave veteran right-hander Pete Fairbanks a one-year, $11 million deal, so there's precedent for Miami spending in that department.

Acquiring a right-handed batter or two after ranking among the worst teams against left-handed pitching last season is also sensible. -- Castillo

New York Mets
The Mets need pitching, starters and relievers. They are the industry favorites to land Tarik Skubal, whom they are scheduled to meet in California next week.

President of baseball operations David Stearns declined to comment on the Skubal pursuit -- or any other free agents -- but he made it clear that adding to the rotation is paramount. The Mets view only Nolan McLean and Christian Scott as locks for the rotation next season.

"Having a complete rotation is really important, and that includes having pitchers that successfully can get you through a playoff series," Stearns said. "We have seen over and over again in the playoffs that it can be constructed in a variety of different ways, and so we're open to doing it any way possible."

The Mets also seek to add to the bullpen after trading four veteran relievers at the deadline. That includes at least one lefty; they've expressed interest in veteran free agents Brooks Raley, Alex Vesia, and Tim Hill, according to sources. They could also add a right-handed-hitting first baseman to platoon with Jared Young. -- Castillo

Philadelphia Phillies
This week, Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski plainly laid out that the team wants to add an outfielder, a utility infielder, rotation depth and a left-handed reliever. Philadelphia has expressed strong interest in Japanese stars Seiya Suzuki and Teruaki Sato.

Suzuki, 32, is an established major league outfielder with a 128 OPS+ in five seasons with the Cubs. Sato is five years younger and coming off a Triple Crown season in Japan, but he hasn't played at this level, and there are real questions about his defense. Though Sato has primarily played third base, he could end up in a corner outfield spot, where the Phillies have a need.

Either player would require another lucrative multiyear deal to add to a roster with eight players already slated to make between $13 million and $42 million next season, though Nick Castellanos' and Taijuan Walker's long-term contracts came off the books. Dombrowski said owner John Middleton is willing to spend money as the Phillies seek a World Series title with this core of veterans before it's too late.

"John's always been tremendous," Dombrowski said. "He's very flexible, but I have a proximate area of what we're going to be. And it's very generous." -- Castillo

Washington Nationals
Washington remains in rebuilding mode after exceeding expectations in president of baseball operations Paul Toboni's first season. That could include trading All-Star infielder CJ Abrams, who is under team control for two more seasons, though that is considered unlikely.

The Nationals' offense was one of the best in baseball, but their pitching, specifically their bullpen, was a disaster. Though they won't engage with any expensive free agents, there is a clear need to upgrade a historically dreadful bullpen that set the major league record for blown saves in a season.

"I think between now and spring training, my guess is there will be a few more faces," Toboni said. "I can't say for sure, but whether that's major league free agency or whatever it might be, trades, I think there might be some movement there. And I think it's good that we'll have that movement." -- Castillo

NL Central

Chicago Cubs
The Cubs have the most free agents in the league, leaving them many spots to fill on the roster. Their main focus, though, will be on the mound.

"We've made no secret we're looking for pitching," GM Carter Hawkins said. "That's been the majority of our conversations [with free agents], and I imagine that will include the trade front as well."

The Cubs won't be in the bidding for Tarik Skubal, but any other pitcher on the market could be part of their plans.

They might get something done this month, before the possible work stoppage, but the bulk of their moves could come in the new year, especially in the bullpen. -- Rogers

Cincinnati Reds
The loss of Emilio Pagan in free agency adds to Cincinnati's urgency on the mound. The Reds' bullpen ERA ranked 25th in MLB, providing for some ugly nights as Cincinnati fell in the standings.

"We'd love to build a bullpen from the back, forward," president of baseball operations Nick Krall said. "We have a handful of open spots. We need to build some depth and some guys on the back end."

The Reds need a lot to augment an offense that got a huge boost from NL Rookie of the Year Sal Stewart. They still need to improve in a few areas around the diamond if they want to stay within striking distance in a very competitive NL Central, but Krall admits it's mostly about pitching. -- Rogers

Milwaukee Brewers
Milwaukee doesn't have many needs, and that's no surprise after winning the World Series.

But the Brewers now have a "target" on their back, according to GM Matt Arnold. That has him doubling down on making sure their processes are in order, even in the first few days after their championship parade.

There will be no resting on their laurels.

"I talk to Pat Murphy about this every day," Arnold said. "I want to make sure we have the right ingredients around our big league team so we can do this again." -- Rogers

Pittsburgh Pirates
Pittsburgh is one of the few teams that essentially has enough pitching to compete. The Pirates will add on the edges, but the organization is ready to take its next step.

The Pirates are also hoping that starter Mitch Keller returns to better form. He missed time because of a shoulder injury, but he should be ready to go in 2027.

"We're bullish on what the pitching group can accomplish," GM Ben Cherington said. "We have a roster that's pretty solid. How do we upgrade it? This offseason, that's a little less specific to a single position and more where are the opportunities?"

In other words, Pittsburgh doesn't have glaring holes for once. A very long rebuild could finally start paying dividends next season, and Cherington's goal is to improve the roster wherever the opportunity arises. -- Rogers

St. Louis Cardinals
St. Louis viewed last season as a success in terms of what the team wanted to do outside of wins and losses -- namely, giving young players runway to advance their games.

Players such as Jordan Walker, JJ Wetherholt and Joshua Baez did just that. Now where do the Cardinals go?

"We'll continue to have lanes for our young players," GM Chaim Bloom said. "There's also looking outside the organization from a trade standpoint to join those players for the long haul. That could be front and center or a supporting role."

The Cardinals believe they're deeper than they were a year ago at this time. It gives them flexibility to improve. A veteran or two in the bullpen would also help stabilize a staff that had some shaky moments in the second half of 2026. -- Rogers

NL West

Arizona Diamondbacks
The D-backs enter this offseason facing a tough question. They have a core group that was good enough to average 85 wins over the past three years, but it didn't make the playoffs in either season. Do the Diamondbacks once again look to supplement it on the margins -- by adding some bullpen help and a much-needed left-handed-hitting first baseman -- or do they break it up?

The D-backs will spend some time exploring the latter option, a source familiar with their thinking said. And the most logical step would be trading Ketel Marte, the talented, enigmatic second baseman who went AWOL on his team last season. The D-backs couldn't find a fit for Marte last winter. Now, he has 10-and-5 rights, giving him the ability to block any trade.

The D-backs have not had formal talks with Marte about a potential trade this offseason, according to a source. That won't come until an offer they deem worthy materializes. But the sense is their bar for Marte, who's 33 and owed $76 million over the next four years, won't be nearly as high as it was a year ago. It can't be. -- Gonzalez

Colorado Rockies
The Rockies are targeting pitching, and lots of it. Though they're not beholden to certain pitch types, they are targeting a specific profile: pitchers who can throw multiple innings. Starters, of course, but also relievers.

"When we were at our best last year, it was probably when we had the most length available," Rockies president of baseball operations Paul DePodesta said. And that length is not geared to the sense of a mop-up guy. It's more like, 'It's 4-3, there's one out in the sixth, go win this for us.'"

Rockies relievers ranked fifth in the majors in innings pitched this season, and though a big part of that is a function of their rotation once again putting up the worst ERA in the majors -- by a lot -- it was also by design. Antonio Senzatela, Chase Dollander, Tanner Gordon, Zach Agnos and others frequently provided multiple innings out of the bullpen. The Rockies need more of those types of pitchers in 2027 because Senzatela was traded at midseason, Dollander underwent elbow surgery, and Gordon and Agnos combined for a 6.33 ERA.

"It's just hard with [13-pitcher roster limits] in our environment to have one-inning guys," DePodesta said. "It's just hard to get through multiple series without roster moves. It's something we'll emphasize. That doesn't mean everybody needs to be a three- or four-inning guy, but we can only afford to have so many one-inning relievers." -- Gonzalez

Los Angeles Dodgers
The Dodgers want Tarik Skubal back, of course. He was an ideal fit in their clubhouse, he's one of the few players who can significantly impact their championship odds, and though they still possess enviable starting-pitching depth, another ace-caliber starter would be ideal, given the injury and workload concerns that consistently surround Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow and Shohei Ohtani.

But Skubal could command a $400 million contract, and the Dodgers don't see themselves going to those lengths given the uncertainty of MLB's economic situation moving forward, sources familiar with their thinking said. The threat of a salary cap in 2028 -- or, more realistically, 2029 or 2030 -- has some Dodgers officials thinking that their only path to landing Skubal might be through a short-term, high-AAV deal, the type he's highly unlikely to accept.

Is there a chance owner Mark Walter, who's facing a federal investigation over alleged self-dealing, approves a nine-figure deal for Skubal? That can never be counted out. But at this point, that does not seem to be on the table. At least not before a potential Dec. 1 lockout.

Outside of Skubal, the Dodgers need to retool their bullpen, and they would like to add a high-end, versatile hitter to their offense, particularly one who can get Freddie Freeman off his feet more frequently at first base. Freeman, one of the faces of the oldest position-player group in baseball, has always been adamant about playing every day. But the Dodgers believe giving him more time off -- as well as third baseman Max Muncy, shortstop Mookie Betts and catcher Will Smith -- can help an older lineup be fresher for the postseason.

The Dodgers are once again open to trading right-handed-hitting corner outfielder Teoscar Hernandez, a move that would create a path for top prospect Josue De Paula in left field, sources said. But if good offers don't present themselves -- they didn't last offseason, and they haven't yet this time around -- they'd prefer to keep him in case De Paula isn't ready defensively in 2027. -- Gonzalez

San Diego Padres
The Padres' new owners, Kwanza Jones and Jose E. Feliciano, want to make a splash this offseason, sources familiar with their thinking have said. In their quest to fill a variety of spots in their rotation, the Padres have set up a meeting with Tarik Skubal but have also expressed interest in Freddy Peralta, among other free agent starters, and are open to reunions with Michael King, Nick Pivetta and Nick Martinez.

"They're committed to putting a winning team on the field," Padres president of baseball operations A.J. Preller said when asked what type of financial flexibility he might have under the new ownership group. "I'm not sure exactly what form that looks like, how much the exact dollars are. I think it's a little bit player-specific. We have some money coming off the books, we have some holes to fill."

The Padres cleared nearly $60 million off their books with Pivetta, King, Jason Adam, Ramon Laureano and Adrian Morejon becoming free agents, but their rotation currently consists of only one starter they can truly depend on in 2027, Randy Vasquez, and they still need to address left field, first base and potentially the back end of their bullpen.

Their payroll is also clogged with massive deals for Manny Machado, Fernando Tatis Jr. and Xander Bogaerts, who combine for more than $80 million annually toward their competitive balance tax payroll -- the one MLB would use for a potential salary cap -- through 2033.

Still, the thought is the new owners will be aggressive.

"I think the biggest thing with Kwanza and Jose is they got a taste of it last year, seeing the team go back to the playoffs, playing a super competitive series in the division series round," Preller said. "We have a core group of position players that we like, that have done a lot of winning, and I think their appetite to put a good team on the field -- they understand it takes resources and it takes payroll to do that." -- Gonzalez

San Francisco Giants
After an aggressive run that saw them extend Matt Chapman, sign Willy Adames and trade for Rafael Devers, the Giants will operate more conservatively this offseason. A 97-loss season will do that.

The Giants will address their pitching staff and look to free agency to do so, but president of baseball operations Buster Posey said "it's going to be harder for us" to sign those who are tied to a qualifying offer and will thus cost them draft picks.

The Giants want to add at least one starting pitcher, and they'll seek multiple relievers to help a bullpen that became a real problem area for them this past season. The Giants probably won't be in the market for Adrian Morejon or David Bednar, but they'll be in on the next tier of free agent relievers.

Generally speaking, they'll hope their expensive veterans rebound and will bide their time until some of their best prospects ascend to the major leagues. -- Gonzalez

stories.headline: Donovan Mitchell's renewed faith in Cleveland fuels the Cavs' future
stories.summary: Mitchell made two commitments this summer: his marriage and his extension with the Cavs. Now it's up to him to keep pushing Cleveland forward.
stories.body:
A FEW WEEKS before Donovan Mitchell and singer Coco Jones were set to be married, they had another reason to rejoice.

It was early July. The pair had gathered for a joint bachelor-bachelorette party before they were officially married in August at a private residence in upstate New York. Seven groomsmen and six bridesmaids joined the couple to commemorate their upcoming nuptials, but Jones and Mitchell took a moment for themselves during the trip. They knew their future was together, and now they were about to solidify where they'd be building it.

The Cleveland Cavaliers were poised to offer Mitchell a four-year, $273 million contract extension that would keep them in Cleveland through 2031. And he was set to sign it, even though he understood that by waiting until next summer, he could earn an additional $80 million.

For years, he had reiterated how much he loved the team and the city. He didn't want a lingering contract negotiation to loom over the 2026-27 Cavs season. He wanted to make the commitment.

"The summer of celebrations," Mitchell told ESPN.

It was a welcome reprieve. His summer was preceded by yet another spring of disappointment.

For the first time in his career, despite making the playoffs in each of his first nine seasons, Mitchell advanced to the conference finals. The Cavs had survived a seven-game first-round series against the Toronto Raptors and then won a Game 7 on the road against the top-seeded Detroit Pistons. Mitchell took it as a sign of growth, that they were finally ready for whatever adversity would arrive. It was Cleveland's deepest run without LeBron James in 34 years.

Then they ran out of gas.

An embarrassing sweep at the hands of the eventual champion New York Knicks finished their 2026 playoff run and left Cleveland with a losing postseason record overall (8-10).

A familiar feeling sat with the franchise.

"In the moment it kind of leaves a sour taste in your mouth," Mitchell told ESPN. "But as you sit ... you have to realize, OK, you've done something you haven't done before. OK. Now that's great, but I wouldn't call it an accomplishment. I would just call it a step."

In Mitchell's four years in Cleveland, the Cavs have consistently been one of the top teams in the Eastern Conference, racking up 51-, 48-, 64- and 52-win seasons.

A regular-season juggernaut. And then a playoff disappointment.

As the Cavaliers entered yet another offseason with the same core, the landscape of the Eastern Conference changed around them.

Rumors of a homecoming with James percolated across the organization and the league, but James chose Philadelphia. In turn, the Cavs bet on continuity, on changes along the margins.

Sources inside and out of the organization said the Cavs weren't interested in trading forward Evan Mobley, who's on a max rookie contract. After acquiring former MVP James Harden at last February's deadline, they re-signed the 37-year-old to a new three-year contract. And one day after the season ended, the team squashed any speculation about the status of coach Kenny Atkinson.

And then Mitchell cemented his commitment.

"When doubt lingers in an organization, it's not great," Atkinson said. "Everybody's just unsettled. So, the fact that Don locked it up, that was huge. It's like a sigh of relief. You know you're going to have your leader and it's going to give you stability. It helps you just move forward quicker."

Their biggest move was acquiring wing Peyton Watson to fill the role as a fifth starter to help protect Mitchell and Harden on defense. So far, their bet hasn't paid off. In fact, the Cavs' starting lineup has a minus-12.0 NET rating this season. Only the starters for Phoenix and Utah have been worse.

It echoes an underwhelming start of the Cavs season. They are 6-6 with skepticism around the league and pundits wondering why this would be any different than Cavs teams that have come up short in years past.

Still, Mitchell made his commitment to the Cavs because he believes in them. But he knows franchises, and especially their superstars, aren't judged by participation trophies.

"For your own mental [health], you have to embrace it and then be proud of that," he said. "In the same token, still keep the motivation of, 'You got your a- swept.'"

THE DONOVAN MITCHELL basketball camp comes to Greenwich, Connecticut, each summer.

For seven of the nine summers since Mitchell entered the NBA, Mitchell has spent a weekend hosting the event for kids from first grade through eighth, in Utah and then now in Cleveland. But he always comes back to the tristate area, where he grew up while his father worked for the New York Mets.

During his camp this offseason, Mitchell knew he was in for it. And the jokes often began with a setup that defined the Cavs' dramatic loss to the Knicks in May.

"Well, analytically ... "

It was a callback to a quote from Atkinson. At a practice before Game 4 of the conference finals, Atkinson said the Cavs were "analytically winning the series" because of expected shot metrics that showed Cleveland actually winning two of three games. Or, in other words, the Knicks were making shots they weren't supposed to make -- and the Cavaliers weren't making shots they were supposed to make.

Still, it made all the wrong headlines.

"You get swept and you look the way we looked, there's criticism and the jokes come with it," Mitchell says. "We all laugh at it, but at the same time it's like, all right, bet. Time's going to come. But hey, you got to live with it. You got to live with all parts of it."

Before a rematch with New York last week, Atkinson attempted to add context to his statement, that he was responding to a question about how the Cavs could still have belief despite trailing 3-0.

"I answered the question as it was taken," Atkinson said. "'You're down 3-0, what hope do you have of even giving your guys?' We get a lot of information, and I wasn't lying in that sense. But in no sense was it like, 'Oh man, we deserve to be winning.' Zero, zero, zero thought of that."

It's a familiar feeling for the Cavs, seeing their words become the story instead of their play.

After losing to the Knicks in the first round of the 2023 playoffs, Allen became a meme for saying "the lights were brighter than expected" after playing at Madison Square Garden.

"That's the world we live in," Cavs guard Sam Merrill told ESPN. "But we just have fun with stuff like that."

That '23 postseason was the first playoff run for Mitchell, Allen and Mobley. They advanced to the second round in the next two seasons before finally cracking the conference finals last spring.

But despite that progress, skeptics around the league point to the same throughline for the Cavs.

"All their questions will be answered in the playoffs," an Eastern Conference executive told ESPN. "But it feels like they have the same issues that have plagued them for years. Not sure what's going to be different."

ON THE MORNING of Oct. 26, Atkinson decided to put an alternative spin on the team's film session before it hosted the Minnesota Timberwolves that evening.

The Cavs had already blown a 29-point lead against the Philadelphia 76ers on opening night, becoming the first team in league history to lose the opener after building a 20-point lead at halftime.

Two nights later, the Cavs saw a 22-point fourth-quarter lead against the Brooklyn Nets get reduced to two with 8.1 seconds remaining; the Cavs held on.

Those blown leads served as a window into the doubt that has followed the team around during the Mitchell era. In Game 1 of the conference finals, the Cavs were ahead by 22 points at Madison Square Garden before collapsing in historic fashion.

Inside the film room, rather than fire up footage from one of the first few games, or even look back at the playoffs, Atkinson turned to a different sport entirely. He had his players watch clips of the England vs. Argentina match from the FIFA World Cup semi-final this past July.

England famously took a 1-0 advantage in the 55th minute, and then completely switched up their play style, falling back into a defensive formation.

Their aggression went cold; the momentum of the match shifted. Argentina rallied to a 2-1 victory to advance to the final.

"[Kenny's] just trying to find ways for it to stick in our head," Cavs forward Jaylon Tyson told ESPN. "It worked."

The Cavs put it into practice that evening. They'd trailed by 15 in the second quarter and double digits at halftime, but after 15 lead changes and five ties in the final minutes, the Cavs survived a 47-point haymaker from Anthony Edwards. Cleveland won in overtime, 127-125.

"There's a lot of belief in this group," Mitchell says. "And the way that we have been able to battle through some adversity and continue to get better and better."

Even still, Cleveland's inconsistency has continued. The Cavs lost by double digits to the Charlotte Hornets on Monday, and then bounced back to beat the Knicks in Madison Square Garden on Wednesday. No one has exemplified their up-and-down season like Harden, now in Year 18, but was brought in to be Mitchell's co-star. Harden is averaging 16.7 points and 5.6 assists while shooting 39% from the field, his lowest marks since he became a full-time starter during the 2012-13 season.

"My name is James Harden, and I used to score a lot of points," Harden said after the Cavs victory in New York. "I still score points, but I'm finding other ways to impact the game as well.

"I'm still trying to figure it out. Donovan averages a lot of points. He's a scoring machine on this team. Just picking and choosing when I have opportunities to score and then do other things to impact winning."

Despite the up-and-down start, the Cavs can look at last season as a reason for patience. They were one game over .500 on Dec. 19, before winning 52 games and securing the No.4 seed.

Mitchell sees the progress through the pain. He sees examples around the league that give him confidence in Cleveland's approach, noting how New York lost in the second round twice and in the conference finals before winning the championship.

"People tend to forget those things," he said. "That how many teams were like, 'Oh, it should be this. This guy needs to be traded. He needs to be fired.'

"All these f----ing things that happen in a lot of championship organizations right before ... "

Mitchell snapped his fingers.

"I'm not saying we're guaranteed to win, but it's just how it's been. So we can't sit here and overreact to s--- just because everybody else thinks you should."

stories.summary: Find game previews, betting intel, broadcast information, stats and highlights here.
stories.body:
After a dizzying array of NHL action Thursday, there are just two games on the schedule for Friday. What's in store for each showdown?

Read on for a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details.

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

New York Rangers at Vancouver Canucks

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NYR -225, O/U: 6.5

Fans of a certain age will recognize this pairing as a rematch of the 1994 Stanley Cup Final, when Mark Messier and the Blueshirts brought the first title since 1940 to Manhattan.

Back to current events, where this will be the final game of the Rangers' four-game West Coast road trip. The swing has included two wins (4-3 over the Kraken and 3-1 against the Flames) as well as a 3-1 loss to the Oilers. Can they earn two more points here?

The Canucks have just three wins this season and have lost six straight. They also didn't seem to push back too hard in a 6-2 loss to the Rangers at Madison Square Garden on Oct. 11.

New York is led in scoring this season by defenseman Adam Fox (22 points through 20 games) and winger Alexis Lafreniere (20 in 20), while center Elias Pettersson (20 in 20) and winger Brock Boeser (17 in 20) are atop Vancouver's slate.

Nashville Predators at Vegas Golden Knights

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | VGK -192, O/U: 5.5

It is not all that surprising that the Golden Knights are in second place in the Pacific Division. They made the Cup finals this past spring and should challenge for the division title until the bitter end.

It's a bit surprising that the Predators are in second place in the Central Division, after they missed the playoffs entirely in 2026 and generally weren't included among the top tier of predicted Western Conference contenders.

But Nashville is on a legit heater right now, bringing a six-game winning streak into this showdown in Sin City. That streak includes wins over the Lightning, Hurricanes and Avalanche, three teams that are considered top Cup challengers.

Vegas is riding a four-game winning streak of its own, albeit including some W's against low-hanging fruit.

The Golden Knights won the first matchup between these teams this season (5-2 on Oct. 13), with five skaters notching goals. Can the Preds slow the Knights' balanced attack Friday?

stories.headline: Rapinoe, Altidore, Ertz into National Soccer Hall of Fame; Beckham gets nod
stories.summary: Former United States national team standouts Megan Rapinoe, Jozy Altidore and Julie Ertz were among those elected to the National Soccer Hall of Fame on Thursday.
stories.body:
Former United States national team standouts Megan Rapinoe, Jozy Altidore and Julie Ertz were among those elected to the National Soccer Hall of Fame on Thursday.

David Beckham, who helped grow soccer in the United States when he joined the LA Galaxy in 2007 and later as an owner of Inter Miami CF, was also voted in on the veteran ballot.

The group announced Thursday will be inducted on April 16 at the National Soccer Hall of Fame in Plano, Texas.

Rapinoe won a pair of Women's World Cup championships, an Olympic gold medal and the 2019 Ballon d'Or during her career. She was also honored with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, in 2022.

She retired from the national team in 2023 with 63 goals and 73 assists in 203 appearances. She also played for Seattle Reign FC in the NWSL from the league's first year in 2013 until her retirement.

Rapinoe was elected on the Hall of Fame's player ballot in her first year of eligibility. Her family, friends, and a group of fans surprised her with announcement of her election upon her arrival off a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.

"To be alongside all the greatest players that have played for us, and played for our country alongside a bunch of my teammates and friends, recognized like that in this way just means you were successful and a part of great teams. So, I definitely was a part of some some great teams, and yeah, it's very special," Rapinoe said in a video posted to social media.

Altidore played in the World Cup twice and scored 42 international goals, to rank third in U.S. history, in 115 appearances for the national team. He also scored the winning goal for Toronto FC in the 2017 MLS Cup championship.

Ertz was considered among the best defensive midfielders in the world before her retirement in 2023. She played in three Women's World Cups and was named U.S. Soccer's Player of the Year twice. She also played professionally for the NWSL's Chicago Red Stars from 2014 to 2021, before a short stint with Angel City FC in 2023.

Known for winning six Premier League titles while with Manchester United, Beckham looms large in the game's growth in the United States. He won back-to-back titles with the Galaxy, scoring 18 goals in 98 appearances. He exercised his option to buy an MLS expansion team in 2014, and Inter Miami joined the league in 2020.

"The National Soccer Hall of Fame recognizes the players and builders who have profoundly shaped the sport," MLS commissioner Don Garber said when he made the announcement to Beckham at a league board meeting. "It is my honor to welcome you to the National Soccer Hall of Fame. Congratulations David."

"This has been an incredible journey. I'm looking to build this league and this sport in this country for a long time. So thank you," Beckham said after learning of his inclusion from Garber.

Tatu, a Brazillian forward who scored 857 regular-season goals over a 21-year indoor soccer career, was also elected to the Hall of Fame on the veteran ballot. He is only the third indoor player to receive the honor.

Former U.S. national team coach Lothar Osiander was elected to the Hall of Fame on the builder ballot. Osiander coached the senior national team in 1986-88 and the Under-23 team in 1988-92. He also had stints as head coach of the then-San Jose Clash and the LA Galaxy.

Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

stories.headline: MMA stars Merab Dvalishvili, Usman Nurmagomedov brawl at hotel in Abu Dhabi
stories.summary: MMA stars Merab Dvalishvili and Usman Nurmagomedov got into a public brawl at a hotel in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday.
stories.body:
Former UFC bantamweight champion Merab Dvalishvili and PFL lightweight champion Usman Nurmagomedov were involved in a physical altercation Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, with video of the incident widely circulated on social media.

Dvalishvili, who is in Abu Dhabi ahead of Saturday's Real American Freestyle event, posted a video of his bloodied face after the scuffle. Multiple videos of the incident showed Nurmagomedov, whose older brother, Umar, lost a bantamweight title fight to Dvalishvili in 2025, approach Dvalishvili from behind and slap him in the face.

Former UFC lightweight champion Ilia Topuria, who is friends with Dvalishvili, shared video of the encounter online. Following the initial slap, Dvalishvili attempts to go after Nurmagomedov. A chaotic scene quickly unfolded, involving multiple members from the camps of both fighters. In his video afterward, Dvalishvili refers to Nurmagomedov and his camp as "snakes."

"What a sneaky way, guys," Dvalishvili says. "What kind of fighters you guys are? What kind of man does this? If you want to try, let's do it the real way."

Abu Dhabi Police issued a statement Thursday, saying eight people were arrested for their part in the brawl, though they did not name Dvalishvili and Nurmagomedov specifically. Additionally, two people who filmed the encounter were also taken arrested. It is not clear whether any or all of the detained parties remain in custody.

UFC president Dana White, speaking at a news conference Thursday, reacted to the altercation, calling it "absolutely ridiculous and stupid."

Wednesday's confrontation marks the latest in a long-running feud between Dvalishvili and the Nurmagomedov team. Before his win over Umar in January 2025, Dvalishvili referred to Umar as "spoiled" and accused the Dagestani of being disrespectful. The two camps were involved in a brief altercation in July at another RAF event in Georgia.

Both Merab and Umar are scheduled to compete at RAF on Saturday. Dvalishvili faces former UFC title challenger Marlon Moraes, while Nurmagomedov will wrestle former UFC champion Urijah Faber.

Usman Nurmagomedov is currently in a state of restricted free agency, with much speculation whether he will leave the PFL to fight in the UFC in 2027.

stories.headline: Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad to continue at Racing Bulls for 2027
stories.summary: Liam Lawson will stay in Formula 1 alongside teammate Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls in 2027, ending weeks of speculation about the New Zealander's future.
stories.body:
Liam Lawson will stay in Formula 1 alongside teammate Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls in 2027, ending weeks of speculation about the New Zealander's future.

Lawson's place at the team had been under scrutiny in recent weeks, with Red Bull's Bulgarian junior Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings.

Racing Bulls ended any doubt on Thursday, confirming Lawson and Lindblad will continue together for another year.

Lawson has been one of the year's standout performers, sitting ninth with 89 points, a run of form which continued with a strong showing at last weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix, where he started third and finished seventh. Rookie teammate Lindblad is 11th with 38.

Racing Bulls is fighting for fifth in the constructors' championship.

- Qatar, Abu Dhabi races set to go ahead as F1 rules out Imola backup plan for finale

- Lewis Hamilton visits Gaza border, urges Israel to 'let the aid trucks in'

Team boss Alan Permane, who last week signed a deal to stay in his role until 2029, said Lawson and Lindblad is the strongest lineup the team could ask for.

"We're delighted to be continuing with Liam and Arvid for 2027," Permane said. "Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we've seen the progress they've made, both individually and as a pairing. I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition.

"Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

Red Bull has confirmed Tsolov as reserve driver for Red Bull and Racing Bulls in 2027. The 19-year-old currently competes in Formula 2 for Campos Racing and is second in the title standings with two races remaining.

The team are promising an "extensive" programme of free practice sessions and Testing of Previous Car running as allowed under the F1 rulebook.

Tsolov said: "I'm incredibly happy and grateful to Red Bull for giving me this opportunity. Since joining the Junior Team, I've received amazing support and have developed so much, both as a driver and as a person. My career has progressed incredibly quickly, and I owe a lot to everyone who has believed in me and helped me get to this point.

"My ambition is clear: I want to become an F1 driver. Having the opportunity to spend next year preparing for that next step is incredibly exciting. I'm confident that with the Team's support and experience, I'll have the best possible preparation to make sure I'm fully ready to take the next step onto the F1 grid when the time comes."

stories.headline: Despite injury and illness, Gus Teixeira is still one of this year's top prospects
stories.summary: Gus Teixeira spent much of his top-age year battling injury and illness, but still found a way to be in contention to be the top pick in the open pool, writes Japser Chellappah.
stories.body:
Gustavo Teixeira had a brilliant top-age campaign. He's worked his way into pick 1 conversations, and is locked into the first handful of selections on draft night.

His success is made all the more impressive considering what's played out behind the scenes.

"I had the ankle injury at the start of the year in the first praccy game," Teixeira tells ESPN.

"It was kind of a bit annoying because every week I thought I'd be playing but it just got pushed back. I had the calf injury, I was out for five or six weeks. I rehabbed that, played a game and then the foot pulled up sore and that's why I'm not testing [at the AFL Draft combine].

"I've also been sick for basically the whole year with a virus."

Teixeira, a powerful forward-half midfielder, played valiantly through glandular fever-like symptoms that didn't get diagnosed until the conclusion of the National Championships.

He was playing games deep in the forward 50 but still finding himself short of breath and unable to hit top gear. After being diagnosed with a severe iron deficiency and receiving an infusion he felt the energy he'd been lacking return, but not before a calf injury linked to his virus took Teixeira out for all but one game in the back half of the season.

Most top-10 chances at the AFL Draft thrive off injury-free seasons where they can continually put their name up in lights. Teixeira couldn't do that this year, so he made his moments count.

His first game back from an ankle concern was in a Vic Metro trial game where he showed his worth, kicking two goals from 20 disposals in a best afield display.

"It was a good day out, I was pretty happy with that. It was annoying I couldn't do a bit more of that throughout the year but I'm sure I can do that in the future."

Teixeira had locked himself into Metro's National Championships outfit by halftime, showing off the power and class that recruiters covet.

At the National Championships he was playing under duress from his undiagnosed virus, but he still took the opportunity to show his value deep in attack.

"Obviously I was sick so I was resting a bit, I was sore the first week and they wanted me to play more forward. I kicked a few goals and they wanted me to stay down forward and that's where I was able to impact the most," he tells ESPN.

Teixeira claimed All-Australian honours, booting seven goals in his four outings including a best on ground demolition of the Allies where he kicked four goals from 22 touches.

It was an element of his game that proved his worth outside of the centre square. Teixeira got to dangerous spots and created separation with proactive running, and from there was able to demonstrate his cleanliness and class to make his chances count.

"I've always thought I want to be a midfielder, I want to play in there. Skills are very important as a midfielder so you've got to be clean and you've got to be able to kick. I'm just chipping away at it and improving."

Teixeira is of Brazilian descent via his father Matt, who was born in the city of Belo Horizonte before moving to Australia when he was 25.

He brings Gus back to Brazil every year, and that connection to a non-English speaking country would allow Teixeira to join zoned club St Kilda's Next Generation Academy if not for friction points within the AFL's own NGA rules.

"Belo Horizonte is just inland of Rio... It's like the size of Melbourne but no one's really heard of it. It's a fully different culture and it's always great to go back," he explains.

"The AFL changed the rules for the regions this year, so they allow South American people this year but you need to be in it for three years. I would've only been in it for a year... my younger siblings are in it now. I've got a brother, Eddie, who's 12 and my sister Lucy who's 14."

Like a host of the top prospects this year, Teixeira has been an Essendon supporter his whole life. The Bombers have the top pick and Teixeira is within that bracket of the pool.

"I haven't thought about the Bombers pick-wise, but just the club and thinking about what it would be like obviously going to the Bombers, it'd be great at the moment. They're getting in some good coaches and they've got some good players coming through.

"Really though I'd be stoked to get drafted to any club, moving interstate would be a pretty cool experience. I'm always trying to get the best out of myself, I've always tried to be the best at everything and just put my best foot forward so I'll do that anywhere."

stories.headline: Dirk Kuyt leaves Fenerbahce a week after defeating Liverpool
stories.summary: Dirk Kuyt left Fenerbahce on Wednesday, one week after guiding the team as interim coach to beat his old club Liverpool in the Champions League.
stories.body:
ISTANBUL -- Dirk Kuyt left Fenerbahce on Wednesday, one week after guiding the team as interim coach to beat his old club Liverpool in the Champions League.

The former Netherlands forward took charge of that 3-2 win in Istanbul despite the club already having made a deal with Emre Belözoğlu to take over.

Kuyt returned in July to Fenerbahce, where he played from 2012-15, to assist coach Ismail Kartal who resigned last month.

"We thank you from the bottom of our hearts for all that you have contributed to these colors," Fenerbahce said in a social media post announcing Kuyt's exit. "Today we say goodbye to you but your place in this big family will never change."

Belözoğlu, a former captain of the club, takes over a team sixth in the Turkish league and 19th in the 36-team Champions League standings.

Fenerbahce's next Champions League opponent is Shakhtar Donetsk in London on Nov. 25.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: Why Kiwi sharp-shooter is taking Cup final personally
stories.summary: Jamayne Isaako is on a remarkable personal run entering the World Cup final, where he has a score to settle with an NRL teammate.
stories.body:
Jamayne Isaako is taking it personally as a generational New Zealand team attempts to break Australia's World Cup stranglehold in their Brisbane decider.

The Kiwis will face the Kangaroos at Suncorp Stadium on Sunday, attempting to win a second cup and first since 2008.

The hosts have won nine of the last 10 tournaments but will be challenged by a side that did everything but win in a 24-22 loss to begin the tournament.

Australian winger Jack Bostock scored a hat trick on debut, twice leaping above Dolphins teammate Isaako for tries while also plucking an intercept.

Isaako, who will leave for the Melbourne Storm next season after 11 campaigns with Brisbane's, Gold Coast's and Redcliffe's NRL clubs, hasn't forgotten.

"Not to take him lightly," Isaako said of what he took from that duel.

"It wasn't something I incorporated into my prep; his height and reach there.

"So it's something I'll be taking personally this weekend, hopefully I can stop him and do a better job."

Bostock played in the centres - on the same side of the field as Isaako - in the New Zealander's last season at the Dolphins and the pair were able to laugh about the contest when they reunited for a photo-shoot this week.

"He gave me a little bit of stick," Isaako said.

The 30-year-old maintains belief is high, pointing to the side's 2023 Pacific Champions triumph as a turning point for the team and himself. The goal-kicker was left out of the Kiwis side for four years before his 2023 return and has played 13 consecutive Test and 98 consecutive NRL games since.

"There's a lot of confidence about what we've been able to create here," he said.

"I don't think we're ever going to get a squad (this good) again, so it's about making the most of the moments we get together.

"I'm certainly going to miss this place (living in Brisbane) and I'd like to finish on a high, hopefully holding the World Cup."
